draft.title: Purposes of sanctions
card: Deterrence discourages crime through fear of a sanction. Specific deterrence aims at the offender, and general deterrence aims at others who might offend.
Punishment makes the offender pay for the wrong, in proportion to how serious the crime was. Denunciation is the court publicly stating that the conduct is wrong.
Rehabilitation helps the offender change, for example through treatment or training, so they do not reoffend. Protection keeps the community safe, for example by keeping the offender in prison.
A sanction can serve several of these purposes at once, and they can pull against each other. The judge weighs them to reach a fitting sentence.
draft.remember: Judges balance five aims: punish, deter, denounce, protect and rehabilitate.

a.q: A court orders an offender to complete a drug treatment program so they can change their behaviour. Which purpose does this mainly serve?
a.why: Treatment aims to change the offender so they do not reoffend, which is rehabilitation. Protection is the tempting wrong answer, but it keeps the community safe by removing the offender, not by changing the person.
a.clue: Which purpose is about changing the offender?

b.q: In sentencing a fraudster to a long prison term, a judge says it should warn others who might commit similar frauds. Which purpose is the judge relying on?
b.why: The warning is aimed at other people who might offend, which is general deterrence. Specific deterrence is the tempting wrong answer, but it aims to discourage this offender, not the wider public.
b.clue: Who is the warning meant for: the offender or others?

check.summary: No problems found. The card matches the five purposes in the Sentencing Act 1991 (Vic) s 5(1), and both questions have one clear right answer that the card teaches.
